reason: Sampling/scheduling policy over ML-processed streams is systems-adjacent and single-GPU, but the contribution is closer to approximate query processing than OS resource management and artifact completeness is unknown.
CPU-only learned index policy runs trivially here, but RL inside an R-tree is a database-index/ML result rather than an OS resource-management problem.
User-space C++ lossy-compression framework with a dedicated artifact repo fits the machine perfectly; headroom is mostly swapping compressors/QoI metrics, a narrower design space.
Mature open-source TVM abstraction that runs on one GPU, but auto-scheduling search is compute-hungry and the work is an ML compiler rather than a core OS topic.
Explicitly single-machine, root-free user-space runtime that schedules validation onto spare cores; only concern is the README's 48-core minimum versus our 16 cores/32 threads.
Actively maintained Rust artifact with a benchmark harness and CPU-only, but SIMD JSONPath query evaluation is far from OS resource management.
LSM-tree indexing in a user-space key-value store is a textbook storage-engine topic with obvious knobs to vary; artifact completeness is unverified from the thin note.
Single-machine ANN index builds fine here but the contribution is a vector-search data structure, not a systems-resource problem, and the note gives no artifact detail.
A comparison study whose baselines are largely multi-GPU/multi-node; the released scripts are a harness, not a system to improve.
AE-badged placement microbenchmark is simulatable on one host, but the headline recovery-speed results need a real multi-disk cluster so only half the evaluation transfers.
Kernel fusion is a genuine single-GPU contribution, but the multi-adapter/pipeline story needs many GPUs and 24 GB caps the fine-tuning scale.
No repo located and it needs an external LLM endpoint; LLM-driven knob tuning is also a DB-autotuning topic rather than core OS.
Tensor-library auto-scheduling works on our Ampere GPU, but part of the evaluation needs a Cambricon accelerator and search-based tuning is expensive in a 10-week budget.

File-system metadata management is squarely OS-relevant and the small-scale claim is testable here, but the scalability half needs several nodes and a full HDFS+DBMS Java stack must be stood up per-user.
Morsel-dispatch policy design space is real multicore task scheduling and runs entirely on 32 threads; the artifact is a Kuzu fork of unknown polish.
Single-GPU schedule primitives are evaluable, but the paper's headline 3D-parallelism results need many GPUs and the main repo is not the artifact repo.
Fully reproduced artifact that runs all parties locally, but the contribution is cryptographic MPC compilation and the WAN half needs root-level link emulation.

Reproduced-badge CUDA/OptiX artifact that the authors already ran on Ampere with 24 GB, so machine fit is excellent; it is GPU-database indexing rather than OS resource management, and profiler-based breakdowns must be replaced by wall-clock timing.
Artifact requirements are below our machine's specs, but the core is online ML retraining for network models with the interesting deployment on an FPGA testbed we lack.

User-space GPU time-multiplexing service with an MLFQ scheduler, explicitly targeting consumer GPUs with no driver changes, plus a separate eval repo — near-ideal for this machine and full of schedulable policy variants.
libCacheSim-based trace-driven eviction policy, CPU-only and root-free, with an explicit overhead/miss-ratio trade-off to attack; only the multi-TB trace corpus needs subsetting.
Lock-free eviction in CacheLib/RocksDB is a perfect 32-thread user-space study; the anonymized repo account with no visible build docs is the main risk.
Well-maintained IntelLabs artifact that fits in 125 GiB RAM, but it is a vector-index library heavily tuned for AVX-512 that our Zen3 host cannot match.
User-space, CPU-only LLVM sanitizer with a shadow-memory encoding is systems-adjacent; the licensed SPEC CPU2017 headline benchmarks must be substituted.
Caching with consistency for serverless is OS-relevant and the topology can be faked with local processes, but a multi-server design collapsed onto one host weakens the headline claims.
No repo, built around a commercial tuner and proprietary telemetry — cannot be built upon, and it is a learned DB-tuning result far from OS topics.
A single-node index-compression benchmark would run perfectly here, but the scout found no artifact at all, which is disqualifying under the hard requirement.
CPU-only JIT/runtime artifact inside NebulaStream is easy to run; adaptive compile-vs-interpret is systems-adjacent runtime work rather than core resource management.
All-CPU compiler on FATE can run as local processes, but the value is cryptographic ciphertext packing and the traffic claims need a real cross-silo link.

Pure user-space memory remapping between parameters and KV cache on vLLM is exactly the OS-flavored LLM-serving topic; multi-tenant results need scaling to small/quantized models and CUDA-wheel/driver-535 compatibility is unverified.
Explicitly designed for a single node with a small memory budget on NVMe, so the I/O-layout and caching design is directly attackable here; hosted under an active vendor org.

The multi-tier checkpoint-loading path from local NVMe to one GPU reproduces directly and is core storage+serving work; the locality-aware scheduler and migration need simulation to stand in for a cluster.
Query routing is scheduling-flavored, but it requires standing up a dual-engine HTAP deployment and the learned dispatcher is a DB-tuning contribution.
No repo located for a CPU numerical library integrated as a DuckDB operator; without code there is nothing to improve.
Time-series storage encoding is a clean single-node Java study, but the artifact is a personal IoTDB fork branch rather than an upstream, documented release.

Intra-device operation overlap is conceptually a perfect single-GPU serving topic with a reproduced, active artifact, but hand-tuned sm_80/sm_90 CUTLASS kernels plus a drop from 70B to 8B mean substantial re-tuning work.
Single-GPU computation reuse with memory-compute compaction is a plausible fit, but inter-frame reuse for video-language models leans ML-application rather than OS.
Model routing under an equivalence constraint depends mainly on hosted model APIs, so there is little local systems mechanism to run or improve on this machine.

Kernel-launch overhead elimination is a real runtime-scheduling problem that is more visible on a modest GPU, but the artifact ships as a CUDA 12.8 Docker image and must be source-built against driver 535.
CPU-GPU attention co-scheduling under SLOs is an excellent OS topic and single-GPU co-location is reproducible, but no repo was located so it fails the hard requirement.
Spatial-temporal prefill/decode sharing is inherently intra-GPU and hostable with a 7B model on the A5000; the repo is new and its completeness is unknown.
Clean CPU-only IBM library with microbenchmarks, but the contribution is an algorithmic data structure rather than systems resource management.
Fusing LM and GNN phases is largely an ML-pipeline contribution, and larger backbones exceed 24 GB so a scaled-down configuration weakens the result.
BitBLAS is a well-maintained Microsoft artifact with an explicit Ladder branch and A6000-class evaluation, but it is a tensor compiler and the FP8/newer-toolkit paths must be dropped on Ampere.

The artifact appendix names RTX A5000 24 GB — the exact GPU here — so the fit is unusually good, but DP training with correlated noise is more of an ML-training/privacy contribution and their box has four GPUs.
The Tuner half (model scaling, job fusion) runs on one GPU, but the Coordinator's heterogeneous-cluster scheduling — the OS-interesting part — must be simulated or dropped.
Concurrent persistent-index construction on a multicore host is a genuine storage-engine topic; the note gives no artifact detail and 'persistent' may imply hardware assumptions worth checking.
User-space Python plus Kvazaar/YOLOv5 runs on one GPU with a clear bandwidth-accuracy knob, but it is a video-analytics application and the live edge-device numbers need Pi/Jetson hardware.
CPU-only learned column compression with an established repo is easy to run and offers many well-defined policy/encoding variants to test.

Checkpoint hashing and I/O reduction are measurable on one node with a user-space Kokkos library, but the HPC cosmology driver must be replaced by synthetic streams and the build chain (Kokkos, io_uring, ADIOS2) is heavy.
Small models on a single GPU are easy to run, but neural cardinality estimation for LIKE-queries is a query-optimizer ML result with little OS content.
SQLancer runs root-free and is a mature codebase, but automated bug-finding for DBMSs is explicitly out of the OS-course sweet spot.
Spark MLlib runs locally and the platform-vs-hyperparameter claim is testable, but the artifact is workload scripts plus cluster traces rather than a system to improve.
Learned stream partitioning is load-balancing flavored, but it is built on Flink and the distributed setting has to be faked with local task managers.

Deliberately avoids vendor profiling tools so it needs no perf counters or root, but it is observability tooling with a visualization front end and the collector may have bit-rotted against current PyTorch.
Textbook eviction-policy work with both a simulator and a Neo4j integration, all user-space; the small personal repo's completeness is the only real unknown.
No preprint and no artifact, and fine-grained GPU/CPU profiling depends on CUPTI counters and perf events that are both admin-restricted on this host.
MIT-licensed user-space runtime drivable with local worker processes, and fault-recovery semantics reproduce; the speedup story is inherently multi-node so absolute numbers will not.
The sub-traversal caching algorithm is genuine cache-design work and trace-drivable, but the headline deployment is a SmartNIC we do not have, leaving only the software vSwitch path.

A simulator explicitly designed to estimate cluster performance from one GPU is a great structural fit and offers many modelling extensions, but its per-server container layer must be ported off Docker to bwrap or plain processes.
Single-GPU persistent-kernel scheduling would fit the A5000 well, but the paper never names a repository so the code location is unknown.
CPU-only with a GitHub plus Zenodo artifact, but a learned cost model for sparse tensor formats and schedules is compiler/ML territory rather than OS resource management.
OrderSage is a reusable released tool, but the empirical result needed 1,700 CloudLab servers and an improvement would be a statistics-methodology contribution validated on one noisy shared host.
Primitive-level dataflow orchestration over a single-GPU engine runs here as-is and offers many schedulable-policy extensions; artifact maturity is unverified.
Offline Shapley attribution over released traces runs on one host, but it is a performance-debugging analysis whose original setting is a production microservice cluster.
QoS-driven request scheduling on the well-maintained Sarathi-Serve base with a named artifact branch; a single-replica scale-down on one A5000 keeps the scheduling mechanism intact.
CPU-only FAISS/HNSW extension that runs trivially here, but hybrid predicate-plus-vector search is an indexing problem with little OS resource-management content.
Single-GPU CUTLASS epilogue fusion is runnable, but SM80-tuned templates need SM86 retuning and the work is a DL compiler contribution.
Best-paper with released code and public RCT data that runs on CPU, but it is closer to a causal-inference data pipeline than a running system, and the trace download is large.
Repo exists and PostgreSQL runs locally, but SFT/RL fine-tuning of an LLM must shrink to fit 24 GB and query optimization is explicitly a low-os_fit area.
Index-based inference inside PostgreSQL is a CPU-only single-node artifact, but the contribution is in-database ML approximation rather than resource management.
Root-free user-space C++/Python trace generator with tunable hit-ratio curves — directly usable for cache-policy work and easy to extend with new workload models.
Single-node C++ learned index on SOSD-style datasets runs easily, but it sits on the ml-for-systems index side rather than a core OS problem and artifact polish is unknown.
Lightweight CPU-only models over PostgreSQL, but index-benefit estimation is a database-tuning ML task matching the low-os_fit anchor.
An out-of-core, I/O-centric single-machine engine would be a good topic, but no repo was located and the largest graph exceeds our 257 GB of free disk.
KV reuse plus length-aware scheduling is an ideal single-GPU OS-flavored mechanism, but no official repo was found so the hard requirement fails.
Only a slice of the design (ghost staging, direction guidance) survives on one GPU; the pipelining core is inherently multi-GPU and the billion-scale datasets exceed 24 GB.
Single-GPU SpMM/SDDMM preprocessing with standard datasets fits the machine, but the repo has no README or description at all and the kernels need an SM86 check.
Dual-queue prefill-length-aware scheduling on SGLang with documented artifact and data; temporal disaggregation on one instance reproduces even though the multi-instance results need several GPUs.
Widely used block-sparse MoE kernels with a fast microbenchmark, but it is a kernel/training contribution built for A100 shared-memory and bandwidth, needing a user-space rebuild without Docker.
